:::{#def-matrix-derivative}

#### Matrix derivative (gradient)

For a scalar-valued function $f(\matr{X})$
of an $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{X}$,
the **matrix derivative** is the $m \times n$ matrix
whose $(i,j)$ entry is the partial derivative of $f$
with respect to the $(i,j)$ entry of $\matr{X}$:

$$
\sb{\deriv{\matr{X}} f}_{ij} = \deriv{X_{ij}} f
$$

Like the vector derivative (@def-vector-derivative),
the matrix derivative is also called the **gradient** of $f$ with respect to $\matr{X}$,
written $\nabla_{\matr{X}} f$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-matrix-derivative}

#### The matrix derivative of a trace

Let $\matr{X}$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix and

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\matr{X}) &= \tr(\matr{X}) \\
&= X_{11} + X_{22}
\end{aligned}
$$

(see [trace](linear-algebra.qmd#def-trace)).
Then $\deriv{X_{ij}} f = 1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise, so:

$$
\deriv{\matr{X}} f = \matr{I}_2
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-deriv-matrix-product-matrix}

#### Matrix derivative of the trace of a matrix product

If $\matr{A}$ ($r \times m$) and $\matr{B}$ ($n \times r$)
are constant with respect to the $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{X}$,
then:

$$
\underbrace{\deriv{\matr{X}} \tr(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})}_{m \times n} =
\underbrace{\tp{\matr{A}}}_{m \times r}
\underbrace{\tp{\matr{B}}}_{r \times n}
$$

:::

::: proof

Write $A_{kl}$, $X_{kl}$, and $B_{kl}$ for the entries of
$\matr{A}$, $\matr{X}$, and $\matr{B}$.
For entry $(i,j)$:

$$
\ba
\sb{\deriv{\matr{X}} \tr(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})}_{ij}
&= \deriv{X_{ij}} \sumto{a}{r} \sumto{b}{m} \sumto{c}{n} A_{ab} X_{bc} B_{ca}
&& \text{(trace of the } r \times r \text{ product } \matr{A}\matr{X}\matr{B} \text{)}
\\
&= \sumto{a}{r} A_{ai} B_{ja}
&& \text{(only the terms with } b = i,\ c = j \text{ depend on } X_{ij} \text{)}
\\
&= \sumto{a}{r} \sb{\tp{\matr{A}}}_{ia} \sb{\tp{\matr{B}}}_{aj}
&& \text{(definition of the transpose)}
\\
&= \sb{\tp{\matr{A}}\,\tp{\matr{B}}}_{ij}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-matrix-product-tensor}
#### Why the theorem uses the trace

The trace makes $\tr(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})$ a scalar,
so its matrix derivative (@def-matrix-derivative) is again an $m \times n$ matrix.
The matrix product $\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B}$ itself
(without the trace) is an $r \times r$ matrix,
and each of its $r^2$ entries has a partial derivative
with respect to each of the $m n$ entries of $\matr{X}$.
Those $r^2 m n$ partial derivatives form a four-index array (a fourth-order tensor),
not a matrix,
which is why this result is stated for the scalar $\tr(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})$.

For example, with

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{A} &= \matr{B} \\
&= \matr{I}_2,
\end{aligned}
$$

the product $\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B} = \matr{X}$ has $4$ entries,
each with $4$ partial derivatives, $16$ in all,
while its trace $X_{11} + X_{22}$ has the $4$ partial derivatives
that form the $2 \times 2$ matrix $\matr{I}_2$ of @exm-matrix-derivative.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-deriv-matrix-product-matrix}

#### Differentiating a weighted trace

Let $\matr{A} = \matr{I}_2$ ($2 \times 2$) and $\matr{B} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ ($2 \times 2$).
Then $\tr(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B}) = 2X_{11} + 3X_{22}$, and:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\deriv{\matr{X}} \tr(\matr{A} \matr{X} \matr{B})}_{2 \times 2}
&= \underbrace{\tp{\matr{A}}}_{2 \times 2} \underbrace{\tp{\matr{B}}}_{2 \times 2} \\
&= \matr{I}_2 \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \\
0 & 3\end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
